name: non-throwing-swap
intent: Give a value-like type an exchange operation that moves only its ownership handles - no copies, no allocation, no fallible user code - and make the no-failure guarantee explicit, so commit and rollback paths such as copy-and-swap assignment can rely on it.
problem: The catalog trigger is "swap must never throw, so rollback paths stay safe": the generic exchange (copy into a temporary, assign both ways) runs the copy constructor, so it can throw precisely where an infallible commit is needed. Whenever an update must be all-or-nothing, the fallible work has to happen before the commit, and the commit itself must be an exchange that cannot fail; a copy-based swap cannot be that step.
context: Types whose representation is (or can be made) a handle to a body - pimpl/handle-body classes, copy-on-write and reference-counted containers, smart pointers, and immutable state objects published behind one reference - plus the generic code that consumes them: standard containers and algorithms (sort, rotate, permutations), copy-and-swap assignment, transactional updates and reloads. The decision is sharp where user-defined copy/move code may throw (C++); elsewhere it collapses into ordinary reference assignment, leaving the discipline "build the new state first, exchange last".
benefits: A commit or rollback step that cannot fail: the fallible part (building the new state) happens before the exchange, so a failed attempt leaves the old state untouched - the strong exception-safety guarantee.
O(1) exchange independent of the size of the represented state: only the handle (pointer, reference, index or body pointer) moves, with no deep copy, no allocation and no resource acquisition.

Uniformity for generic code: one swap that is found both unqualified (ADL) and qualified (std::swap or the language's generic swap) means algorithms, containers and copy-and-swap assignments all get the efficient version instead of the generic copy-based fallback.
Resource ownership changes hands in one step: the old representation is released by the destructor of the temporary that received it, so cleanup stays on one path.
Cheaper derived operations: move assignment, shrink-to-fit, clear-by-swap, double-buffering and hot-reload of state all reduce to the same non-throwing exchange.
tradeoffs: The guarantee is a promise the callers cannot see: if the swap actually performs fallible work (allocation, logging, callbacks, taking a lock, copying another object) then a noexcept/declared-infallible swap turns a recoverable error into std::terminate or into a corrupted rollback path.

It only pays off when the representation is a handle: for types whose state lives inline, the exchange still copies every field, and the non-throwing property is inherited from the members rather than created here.

The whole representation must move together: fields added later (caches, observer lists, back-pointers, indices, mutexes) that are not exchanged leave an object half old and half new - a silent invariant break.

External aliases survive the exchange: references, iterators, pointers and observers into the old body keep pointing there, which is the intended sharing behaviour for a copy-on-write handle and a bug for a value that callers assume is updated in place.

The home language's protocol is easy to get subtly wrong - member swap vs free swap vs std::swap specialization, ADL vs qualified calls, the class-template specialization ban, self-swap - and easy to "simplify" back into the copy-based version.
Where the exchange is already primitive, wrapping it in a helper or abstraction (a Swap class, a closure, a tuple) adds indirection and allocation without adding any guarantee.

participants.responsibility: Owns the representation and defines what exchanging it means; keeps every piece of state that must travel together inside the handle so an exchange can never leave a partially updated object.
The pointer, reference, index or state object that is actually exchanged; it must be cheap to move and free of fallible work, which is what makes the swap non-throwing.
The member swap and the matching non-member (ADL) swap: the customization point that exchanges handles only, is declared or known not to fail, and is the only thing clients are allowed to rely on.

The uniform lookup and dispatch path - std::swap and the Swappable requirement in C++, multiple assignment, destructuring or a standard-library swap elsewhere - so callers never need to know which type has a custom swap.

Copy-and-swap assignment, transactional update, container algorithm or hot reload: performs all fallible work first and uses the swap as the infallible commit, so a failure leaves the previous state in place.

use_cases: Copy assignment implemented as copy-and-swap: build a temporary copy (the only fallible step), then exchange it with *this so the old state is released by the temporary's destructor.
Handle-body / pimpl classes whose swap exchanges one implementation pointer - the classic realization and the reason the idiom exists.
Copy-on-write and reference-counted containers: the commit step replaces the shared body with a freshly built one while readers of the old body stay valid.
Shrink-to-fit and clear-by-swap: Container(container).swap(container) releases capacity without disturbing the elements' storage semantics.
Rollback of an in-progress update: stage a modified copy (or a new state object) and exchange it into place only after every step succeeded; the previous state is still intact if anything failed.

Concurrent publication of an immutable snapshot: readers take the current state and the writer exchanges one reference (atomic exchange / AtomicReference / Interlocked.Exchange / atomic.Pointer) so no reader sees a half-installed state.
Standard algorithms and containers that require swappable elements: sort, rotate, permute and unique rely on the exchange being cheap and, in their strong-guarantee overloads, non-throwing.
Qt's QSharedDataPointer provides an explicit swap() documented as a fast, noexcept exchange for implicitly shared value classes, making the shared-data handle the commit unit.
C++ std::vector::swap exchanges contents and capacity in constant time without moving or copying elements; allocator propagation and equality conditions still govern its no-throw contract.
C++ std::shared_ptr::swap exchanges stored pointers and ownership in constant time without changing reference counts during the swap, providing a concrete smart-pointer handle exchange.
avoid_when: The type is trivially copyable or cheap to move (an int, a small struct, an array of them): the ordinary exchange already cannot fail, so a hand-written swap is noise.

The representation cannot be exchanged cheaply - the state lives inline and would have to be copied, or the object owns things whose ownership cannot be transferred (references to itself, registered observers, OS handles with callbacks) - fix the representation (introduce a handle) before claiming a non-throwing swap.

The exchange genuinely needs to do fallible work (take a lock, allocate, register a callback, write a log): do not declare it non-throwing; keep the commit as a single reference assignment instead, or accept an explicit failure path.

The language has no user-defined value semantics and no throwing assignment (Java, Python, Ruby, Go, JS/TS, C#): wrapping the exchange in a helper adds nothing; rely on the primitive and keep the state behind one reference.
Swapping is being used to dodge a design problem - to copy an object that should have been replaced, or to paper over aliasing between two objects - rather than to commit a new state.
anti_patterns: A "non-throwing" swap built on the copy-based exchange (temporary copy, two assignments): it allocates through the copy constructor and can throw - the exact implementation the pattern replaces, and the reason a copy assignment implemented with it gives no strong guarantee.

Declaring swap noexcept while its body calls something that can throw (member assignment, container growth, logging, a user callback, mutex acquisition): any escape terminates the program, so the "safety" becomes a crash.
Exchanging only part of the representation - swapping the pimpl pointer but not the cached size, the body's back-pointer or a mutex - leaving the object half old and half new.
A swap that deep-copies owned resources instead of exchanging handles: it can throw and it defeats the O(1) point of the pattern.

The XOR/arithmetic swap trick (a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b) presented as the no-temporary alternative: it only exists for integers and pointers, reads worse, and creates no guarantee whatsoever - it is a puzzle, not the pattern.

A generic "swap anything" helper that silently falls back to copying when no custom swap exists: it restores the throwing copy-based path invisibly and discourages types from declaring their own non-throwing swap.
design_principles: Fail fast, then commit infallibly: do all fallible work first and make the final step an operation that cannot fail.
Single responsibility: the swap moves ownership handles; construction, validation and resource acquisition stay in their own steps.
Invariant preservation: exchange the whole representation at once so no observer can see a partially updated object.
Honesty in interfaces: the no-failure guarantee is part of the type's contract (noexcept or documented) and must not be claimed when the implementation can fail.
Zero-overhead abstraction: exchanging handles should compile to a few register moves, not to a copy of the represented state.
Uniformity for genericity: one protocol (ADL plus the generic swap, or the language's own primitive) so generic algorithms never fall back to a degrading implementation.
best_practices: Give the type a member swap (or a friend/ADL non-member swap) that exchanges handles only and mark it noexcept; provide the non-member in the class's namespace as well, and for non-template classes a std::swap specialization, so both qualified and unqualified calls find the efficient version (Effective C++ Item 25).
In generic code always write `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` so argument-dependent lookup can pick a user-defined swap while the standard one stays the fallback.
Keep fallible work (building the copy or the new state) outside the commit step; implement copy assignment as copy-and-swap and move assignment as a swap with the donor.
Pin the guarantee with a compile-time check (static_assert(std::is_nothrow_swappable_v<T>), or the equivalent trait) so a later refactor cannot silently re-enable a throwing path.
Keep everything that belongs to the value inside the exchanged handle - caches, back-pointers, size, ownership - and handle self-swap and aliased handles explicitly.

Where instances are shared between threads, exchange one immutable state reference atomically (atomic exchange, AtomicReference, Interlocked.Exchange, atomic.Pointer) rather than swapping two independent fields.

Prefer the language's own exchange primitive when one exists (mem::swap and mem::replace in Rust, swap/swapAt in Swift, multiple assignment or destructuring in Python, Ruby, Go, JavaScript and C#) instead of re-implementing the C++ protocol.
